Latest Yorkers are coming to terms with the unenviable conditions they’ve voted themselves into, with some experiencing sticker shock and a commensurate degree of buyer’s remorse. Who could blame them? The response from Democrats to the public’s frustrations should only further reinforce the unavoidable conclusion that New Yorkers have populated city government with neophytes and ignoramuses.

Fresh York Times reporter Emma Fitzsimmons could not have anticipated the garment-rending apoplexy that her social media post would inspire in city officials. Nevertheless, she fulfilled her reportorial duties when, after completing her Amazon.com purchase of a children’s liquid vitamin, she encountered this message from the online retailer: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order,” it read. “Act now to protect low prices.”.

Noah Rothman is a senior writer at National Review. His third book, Blood and Progress: A Century of Left-Wing Violence, was published by Hachette in May 2026.

We need your help to stay independent.

This is the dinner for when I want something cozy and substantial but do not want to peel a single potato.

Industry observers note that brown ground beef or chicken in a skillet with frozen onions, garlic and mushrooms. Once everything has developed some color, stir in a brown or mushroom gravy packet, a splash of stock and a generous quantity of frozen mixed vegetables.

Let the filling simmer until thick and savory, then transfer it to a baking dish (or keep it in an oven-safe skillet, if you have one). Spread deli-counter mashed potatoes over the top and bake until the filling is bubbling and the potatoes are golden in spots.

Hearty, comforting and full of vegetables, without having to peel, chop or mash a thing.

Recent findings suggest that the beans bring both flavor and fiber, the sausage adds richness and heat, and the spinach practically disappears into the sauce. I would happily eat this again tomorrow.

This is the sort of thing I love making when I want something fresh, bright and satisfying without spending much time at the stove.

Cook some small pasta â Iâm fond of cubetti here â and add frozen peas and carrots, cooking them just long enough to heat through. Drain, cool slightly and toss with canned white beans and a generous amount of Sauz Lemon Pepper Pesto.

You can eat it slightly warm or chill it for later. Either way, the creamy, lemony pesto ties everything together, while the vegetables and beans make the whole thing more substantial.

Latest Update: America and China Are Trying to Alter Their Economic Bargain

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
  • Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy.
  • Recent findings suggest that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

According to recent reports, the United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

Recent findings suggest that the United States and China are locked in a derisking race. After decades of actively entwining their economies, both are now trying to achieve a degree of separation between them. Neither side seeks at this point to decouple completely from its rival. Each is trying instead to alter the terms of their economic relationship, reducing their own vulnerability to leverage, coercion or attacks that could damage its long-term prosperity and security, while working to acquire advantages over its counterparty. This is a struggle for power, waged through trade, investment and technology development.

Today’s derisking race signals the failure of the third attempt by the United States to build an open, fully integrated world economy. At the end of the Cold War, as after the two world wars, American policymakers were motivated by a mix of pragmatism and principle. They believed that there were enormous gains to be had from trade with large and potentially fast-growing markets. But they also hoped to bring to fruition the liberal dream of a ‘one-world’ global trading system in which freer flows of goods, capital and people would promote peace and freedom, as well as prosperity.

In a recent development, in 1919 America had the world’s biggest economy, but the international political system was still multipolar, with other great powers in both Europe and Asia. Although Woodrow Wilson tried to persuade the victors, and his own people, of the wisdom of lowering tariff barriers and creating an open global trading system, both at home and abroad he lacked the ability to compel others to accept his ideas. Once rebuffed, America drew back into isolationism and protectionism. With no nation willing and able to hold it together, in the 1930s the global economy split apart.

In a recent development, by 1945 the world had become bipolar, with the United States and the Soviet Union standing above all other nations—and America alone briefly accounting for as much as half of global GDP. American planners at first entertained hopes of reviving Wilson’s vision, but the onset of the Cold War soon forced them to abandon the idea. Instead of cooperating to create a single unified system, each superpower proceeded to build its own largely separate bloc. Organised along predominantly liberal, free-market lines, the American-led bloc was ultimately able to out-produce, out-innovate, and out-last its Communist opponent.

With the demise of its former rival, the United States finally seemed set to restructure the entire world economy into a unified trading system. America and its allies hoped in the process to encourage the domestic transformation of their former enemies, preparing them to become members in good standing of what would finally be a globe-spanning liberal order.

The main instrument of this strategy in the economic realm was the World Trade Organization, and its most important target was China. To gain entry to the WTO China was required to make detailed commitments that, if followed, would bring its economic policies into closer alignment with liberal principles of open markets, limited state intervention and freer trade.

Political change was expected to follow close on the heels of economic liberalisation. Increased reliance on markets would lead to rising prosperity and, as had already happened in Western Europe and parts of Asia, the members of an expanding middle class would demand political rights to go with their growing economic freedoms.

It has been revealed that american strategists knew that drawing China more fully into an expanding world economy would enable it to accumulate power as well as wealth. But they were reassured by the conviction that prosperity would eventually bring democratisation, and by the knowledge that democracies had seldom gone to war with each other.

It has been revealed that for their part, China’s rulers saw the West’s offers of engagement as a trap designed to bring about their own demise. Instead of succumbing to the charms of liberalism, they remained firmly committed to a mercantilist-Leninist governing philosophy, in which the primary purpose of economic activity is not to enhance the welfare of the Chinese people but to bolster the power of the Party and, through it, the nation.

Industry observers note that thus, even as it allowed greater play to market forces, the CCP regime took care to ensure its continued grip at home. And it approached the global economy as another domain of zero-sum struggle, one in which the aim was to strengthen China’s geopolitical position and gain advantage over its rivals.

Sources indicate that for a time, the nation’s leaders believed they had little choice but to accept the dangers of increasing interdependence with the West. Once having obtained membership in the WTO, however, Beijing began to take steps to reduce its vulnerability to foreign pressure.

After the turn of the century this derisking strategy advanced along four parallel axes:.

In a recent development, to guard against the possibility of being cut off from vitally needed imports of resources and raw materials, Chinese companies were directed to buy up more overseas mines, oil wells and agricultural land and to build a vast merchant fleet and an elaborate global network of roads, railways and ports to carry their output back home. To reduce exposure to Western tariffs or trade sanctions, Beijing sought fresh export markets in the global south. To blunt the impact of U.S. financial sanctions, it began to build alternative international payments systems. Finally, to lessen dependence on imported technology China rolled out a series of costly, high-profile technology development programs, began buying cutting-edge Western companies and initiated a campaign of industrial espionage of unprecedented scope and scale.

Recent findings suggest that from the end of the Cold War until the mid-2010s, Washington continued to try to ease Beijing down the path towards economic liberalisation. Together with this persistence, however, there was mounting frustration over China’s trade and industrial policies and its evident failure to live up to the commitments it had made to gain entry to the WTO. As the Chinese economy grew and its level of technological sophistication advanced, these policies appeared to threaten the future prosperity and security of the United States and other industrial democracies.

China’s heavily subsidized exports were hollowing out portions of the American manufacturing base. Relatively easy access to Western companies and universities was helping to speed its technological advance. Its ongoing military buildup and more assertive foreign policy stance darkened perceptions of its intentions and began to make it appear less as a normal trading partner and more like a strategic rival and even a potential foe. Despite all of this, it was not until the very end of Barack Obama’s second term that China’s increasingly forceful efforts to strengthen its position finally began to provoke a meaningful response.

Washington’s belated answer to China’s mercantilist, power-maximising economic policies signalled the start of a two-sided derisking race. The American reaction came first in the form of the experimental and at times spasmodic initiatives of the first Trump administration and then the more coherent, but also limited and cautious approaches pursued by the Biden administration.

Recent findings suggest that neither Trump nor Biden sought to decouple completely from China, nor did either of them formally abandon the original, ambitious goal of creating an open global economy. Nevertheless, albeit with some hesitation, at least with respect to China the United States started to move away from a predominantly liberal approach to economic relations that emphasized the virtues of openness and the prospect of mutual benefits, towards one that increasingly prioritized power and the pursuit of relative advantage.

America’s derisking campaign comprised several interrelated lines of effort. Regardless of cost, it no longer seemed prudent to depend on a potentially hostile China for minerals, drugs, metals, and chemicals that might be needed in a war or national emergency. To reduce the dangers of dependence, the United States began to use tariffs to constrict imports and subsidies to cultivate alternative sources of supply.

Once seen as a benign byproduct of globalization, the pervasive presence of Chinese-made electronic components and hardware in America’s critical networks now appeared to pose unacceptable risks of espionage or sabotage. Dealing with the problem of penetration by removing these imported products and replacing them with reliable substitutes called for newly introduced laws and regulations to guide private companies and government agencies. Finally, slowing the transfer of sensitive technologies required imposing tighter controls on exports and on investment flows both to and from China.

Beijing has reacted to these developments by doubling down. Xi Jinping’s determination to stay the course is due in part to the fact that America’s tougher policies did not come as a surprise. Back in 2002, in the wake of China’s accession to the WTO and the 9/11 attacks, CCP strategists had concluded that they faced a “twenty-year period of strategic opportunity” during which they could grow strong without undue interference from Washington.

In a recent development, eventually, however, the Americans would turn their attention back to China and, recognizing how much it had grown, they would try even harder to weaken and contain it. At that point Beijing would have no choice but to press ahead.

Sources indicate that in the past five years, China has done more to increase security of supplies of food and raw materials, diminish its exposure to financial sanctions, and increase the relative importance of the developing countries as markets for its exports. Together with these defensive measures Beijing has begun to take more aggressive actions. Rather than implement reforms that might have reduced exports and lessened tensions with other nations, it has moved in the opposite direction: ratcheting up subsidies, expanding manufacturing capacity, and boosting exports that threaten to destroy others’ industries and leave them even more reliant on Chinese goods. Chinese firms are also working to dominate global supply chains for critical minerals and other industrial materials. The regime has successfully used the threat of export restrictions on rare earth minerals to pressure America and its democratic partners and is actively seeking to tighten its grip on other potential “chokepoints.”.

Industry observers note that the U.S. rejoinder to this intense and purposeful campaign has been mixed and less than fully coherent. Since his return to the White House Donald Trump has expanded on some of the policies that he set in motion during his first term, but he has also taken steps that threaten to undermine their effectiveness.

The second Trump administration has prohibited the importation of Chinese-made drones, robots, and internet routers that could be connected to U.S. telecommunications networks. But it has also ignored the law banning TikTok, a Chinese-controlled social media platform suspected of gathering sensitive information and spreading propaganda, instead negotiating a sale to one of Trump’s domestic political allies.

To lessen dependence on China, the administration has sought to work with other countries to develop alternative sources of critical minerals. At the same time, in hopes of reviving American industry, it has strained relations with its allies by imposing across-the-board tariffs on their exports, driving countries like Canada closer to Beijing. Finally, since returning to office, Trump has tightened certain restrictions on high tech exports to China while simultaneously loosening export controls on advanced semiconductors crucial to the development of artificial intelligence.

In a recent development, china’s course in the next stage of the derisking race seems set but America’s remains uncertain. The history of the past century suggests two alternative trajectories. Having failed once again to build a fully integrated global order, the United States may choose not only to distance itself from China but to adopt a posture of omni-directional protectionism and strict “America first” industrial policy as it did after World War I. This risks leaving America isolated as its former friends band together to protect themselves from its own predatory policies as well as China’s.

Recent findings suggest that the aftermath of the Second World War suggests a preferable alternative. Instead of completely abandoning liberal economic principles, Americans could decide instead to narrow the circle in which they are applied to include only those nations that genuinely share and are prepared to defend them. It is only by pooling their resources and better integrating their markets that the advanced democracies can counter a challenge of unprecedented proportions.

Aaron L. Friedberg is a professor emeritus of politics and international affairs at Princeton University. His most recent book is The Derisking Race: China, America, and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.

On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â.

Sources indicate that voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

Recent findings suggest that trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â.

It has been revealed that in the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â.

Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

In a recent development, critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â.

In a recent development, trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on key commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â.

Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â.

It has been revealed that in a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

In a recent development, albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â.

But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â.

Like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â.

In a recent development, political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â.

According to recent reports, the children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â.

In a recent development, the election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â.

But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â.

Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â.

Industry observers note that an election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

We need your help to stay independent.

In a recent development, the Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â.

In a recent development, political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more notable than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â.

It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

Breaking: The U.S. Tech Outage Wave, Explained

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on.
  • federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

A wave of tech outages in the U.S. federal government and private sector over the past week have made a lot of people understandably nervous. The outages affected commercial air travel, email, banking, and more—in some cases causing disruptions worldwide.

A global Microsoft outage that began last Thursday derailed a number of services that businesses, schools, and governments rely on. Then the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday leading to widespread flight cancellations and delays. Chase Bank, Bank of America, and Apple services also faced brief disruptions in recent days. And on Tuesday, some internal systems at the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

Given the outages occurred on such a massive scale and in quick succession, questions have been raised as to whether they were a result of nefarious activities. But there is at the moment no evidence that the recent incidents were due to cyberattacks or that they were linked.

The Microsoft outage was the result of a combination of factors, including a “latent bug” from July that caused servers to become “overwhelmed and unresponsive,” Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, agents, and platform, said in a post on X. Lamanna said a “surge in load” and decreased server capacity had also contributed to the outage.

Recent findings suggest that the FAA is still assessing what led to the ground stop, which lasted less than five hours, but a preliminary investigation indicated that the technical problem was caused by the installation of a router at a radio facility in Arkansas that may have flooded its communications network. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, is also being looked at as part of the inquiry.

The short-lived Chase Bank outage on Monday, which led to issues with processing transactions and seemingly had a ripple effect that caused problems for customers at other banks, was the result of a “software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” the bank noted in a post on X, adding that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” Apple said the outage it experienced on Tuesday, which lasted hours and disrupted the Apple Store and other services, was the result of an “internal revision” and not due to a cyberattack.

According to recent reports, the NSA disruption, which reportedly caused the agency’s internal communications network for highly classified information, NSANet, to go offline, had a similarly prosaic cause. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”.

The Trump administration has acknowledged the unease the outages have caused among the public while emphasizing that there are currently no indications that any were tied to a cyberattack or coordinated by outside actors.

Industry observers note that “I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. “But based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday recognized that people are “fearful” and “uncertain,” but he was unequivocal: “We are not under systemic attack,” he remarked. “These events—one has nothing to do with the other. They are not interrelated.”.

According to recent reports, but it makes sense that people are on edge about technology and how its dominance over modern life can make societies vulnerable. All of these incidents came on the heels of a series of suspected cyberattacks on supermarket freezers in Europe that caused millions of dollars in damage. They’ve also come at a time when anxiety over the rapid development of artificial intelligence has reached a fever pitch.

It doesn’t help that these outages hit as the increasingly symbiotic relationship between AI and the stock market was on many people’s minds amid the chaos swirling around Nvidia—following a salacious scandal that led to the resignation of the tech giant’s co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang.

And national security and tech experts say AI may be partly to blame for these disruptions—though not in the way you might think. AI tools are increasingly helping organizations to identify vulnerabilities in their computer systems. That’s mostly a good thing because those flaws can then be fixed before any potential bad actors can exploit them. But those fixes don’t always go smoothly.

“AI code scanning has caused a tidal wave of vulnerability discovery,” and companies and government agencies are “rushing to make updates and fix” those vulnerabilities, David Agranovich, a director for intelligence on the National Security Council during the first Trump administration, remarked in a post on X. “[E]specially with legacy infrastructure, it can be incredibly hard to predict all of the different dependencies that might break because of those patches. The pace of manual patching has a cost, and that cost is reliability,” Agranovich added. “The result is many cascading and disparate system outages.”.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, offered a similar assessment. Warner noted in a statement on Tuesday that he understood why Americans were so concerned about the widespread outages and underscored that there is “no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort.” But he added that what appears to be happening is a “consequence of how promptly artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape.”.

AI has opened the door to “identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner stated.

The recent disruptions should serve as a “wake-up call” on the ways in which AI is “moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said, reiterating his call for “commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections.”.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan plan Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Sources indicate that van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a blueprint from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

“I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen stated. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a new suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move rapidly.

Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

At the earlier appearance, Daines said that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

“We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines said.

Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

But Democrats have been debating whether to use their upcoming majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

It has been revealed that democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines plan.

Schumer has remarked he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

“I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the big things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen said.

Sources indicate that senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

The “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

It has been revealed that the first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

Sources indicate that in 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

Recent findings suggest that I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

According to recent reports, so I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â.

Recent findings suggest that but a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

We need your help to stay independent.

The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of Latest Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just stated for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

It has been revealed that chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a latest one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

It has been revealed that when Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

In a recent development, over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

Sources indicate that the history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

According to recent reports, the business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Sources indicate that thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Sources indicate that thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

According to recent reports, welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a major hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Chinese President Xi Jinping’s APEC agenda, an Iranian attack on a U.S. military base in Kuwait, and the European Union’s latest loan to Ukraine.

Recent findings suggest that chinese President Xi Jinping is just warming up for his highly anticipated trilateral summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump on Thursday. From delivering a pointed speech that criticized “unilateralism and protectionism” to breaking protocol with a massive hug for Trump on the tarmac, Xi appears to be showing the world that he is eager to hold the diplomatic reins.

According to recent reports, the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit kicked off in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday with a two-hour meeting between Xi and Putin. During the talks, Xi highlighted the importance of the China-Russia relationship and touted the necessity of a multipolar world.

Recent findings suggest that in a keynote address later that day, he further vowed to defy trade protectionism and maintain a “free and open” system, painting Beijing as a stable economic partner that can counter the White House’s volatile tariff war. Putin echoed that message in his own speech while criticizing Western sanctions imposed on Russia due to its war against Ukraine.

It has been revealed that the meetings and speeches did not signal a dramatic shift in policy; Xi has already used this week’s Asia-Pacific summitry to curry favor with some of the region’s most influential allies, from Canada to Peru. However, the timing was notable, as just a few hours after the Xi-Putin talks, Xi was on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to personally greet Trump with a warm embrace.

It has been revealed that such a personal welcome is uncommon for the Chinese president, who usually sends a high-level representative to meet with foreign leaders when they touch down in China. However, the friendly greeting may be an effort to parallel Trump’s own approach to their relationship, as Trump met Xi at the bottom of the stairs to his jet when the latter flew to Washington in September.

It has been revealed that wednesday’s red-carpet welcome for the U.S. president also included an honor guard, a military flyover, an array of flowers, and a cheering crowd. Trump “loves pomp and circumstance, and these kinds of events present an incredible opportunity there,” Mike Kuiken, the vice chair of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar ahead of Trump’s Asia trip. “[T]his is the kind of thing that plays to his insecurities in a way that he’ll very much enjoy,” Kuiken added.

Recent findings suggest that xi later hosted Putin, Trump, and the other gathered dignitaries at an APEC welcome banquet, during which the Chinese leader outlined the primary goals of the summit. “We will discuss steps to expand mutual openness, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, extend opportunities for result-oriented cooperation across various fields, and strive to deliver more tangible results on the ground,” Xi stated.

As for what will be on the agenda for Thursday’s trilateral meeting, Trump has stressed his interest in discussing the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as nuclear disarmament; however, experts expect Xi to try to steer the conversation away from nuclear arms collaboration.

Putin, meanwhile, appears optimistic about Thursday’s dialogue, insisting that the talks will likely have a significant impact on global affairs. “I therefore expect massive potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting,” Putin stated.

According to recent reports, widening strikes. Iranian forces targeted a U.S. air base in Kuwait on Wednesday for the first time since September, upending a roughly two-month pause on strikes against U.S. military sites. That same day, Tehran also introduced several attacks on Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. Both small Persian Gulf countries claimed to have intercepted Iran’s aerial assaults.

Industry observers note that wednesday’s strikes marked the latest round of tit-for-tat attacks between Iran and the United States. According to Iran’s military, the operation against Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base on Wednesday was in retaliation for a U.S. airstrike on Iran’s Qeshm Island the day before. Qeshm serves as a staging ground for Iranian forces targeting global shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, and it hosts an expansive underground tunnel network that is often used as a base of operations for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

In a recent development, “If ​the enemy repeats its mistake,” Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami stated in a video posted by state media on Wednesday, “we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.” Such a threat comes one day after seven U.S. officials told CNN that Tehran is considering detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside Washington to target senior Trump administration officials. The White House has stressed that there is no imminent threat to the U.S. homeland.

In a recent development, strapped for cash. The European Commission proposed a latest $49.5 billion loan to Ukraine on Wednesday to help Kyiv avert its looming cash crisis and bolster its defenses against Russia. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiating table,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen remarked. “And Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine.”.

Industry observers note that last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined a $76.8 billion funding gap for 2027, at a time when Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure. Notably, Moscow is expected to double its drone deployments next year to 20 million units, which EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said will likely force Kyiv to allocate some 62 percent of its military budget on drones.

A nearly $50 billion EU loan will cover roughly two-thirds of this gap; aid will be split between weapons funding and civilian needs, such as for hospitals and schools, and foreign allies will be encouraged to supply the rest. Von der Leyen expressed confidence on Wednesday that all 27 EU member states will support the loan. However, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Slovakia have already noted that they will not take part in the latest funding round, prompting Germany to threaten to veto the bloc’s seven-year budget until all nations are on board.

Recent findings suggest that AI cheating concerns. Around 550,000 South Korean students are preparing to take their university entrance exam, known as the Suneung, at more than 1,300 testing centers across the country on Thursday. The high-stress event is known for causing minor disruptions to businesses, as traffic is redirected, offices and tourist attractions open later, and extra trains run to accommodate test-taking.

However, this year’s exam will also include latest restrictions to crack down on potential cheating after the top scorer of another professional test admitted on Sunday to using artificial intelligence to secure his suspiciously high score; the individual only got one question wrong on the tax accountant exam by using a miniature camera, a phone, and AI.

Recent findings suggest that the admission prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to convene an emergency cabinet meeting this week to discuss what the prime minister described as the “social evil” of AI-empowered fraud. “Cheating on exams using advanced equipment is no different from stealing the scores of hundreds of thousands of examinees who worked hard,” Lee wrote on X on Tuesday.

It has been revealed that among the new testing measures, all smartphones will be confiscated, glasses and watches will be inspected, and some public Wi-Fi spots will be blocked. A reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) will also be given to anyone who reports an instance of cheating involving advanced equipment.

According to recent reports, A packed week of high-stakes summitry has kept Trump busy and, perhaps, hungry. But Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. believes that he has the perfect solution. The host of this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations conference arranged for the U.S. president to receive a late-night delivery of Jollibee fried chicken on Wednesday as a sort of pick-me-up after a hard day’s work. Jollibee is the Philippines’s most popular fast-food chain and represents what Marcos described as a “taste of Manila.”.

FP’s World Brief writer would like to note that she too has been kept busy and famished by this week’s onslaught of news and would also enjoy some Jollibee fried chicken if Marcos wants to put in a second order.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

“I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

Recent findings suggest that democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also noted Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

Sources indicate that ueland remarked if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

“It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

Democrats stated Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

Industry observers note that ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

It has been revealed that democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

Ueland did not give a direct response.

“First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

He also remarked it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

Peters noted when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

According to recent reports, “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters stated. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

“That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

Ueland said his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

Ueland said he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

For example, he said GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

Ueland remarked he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland noted, “To be clear, yes.”.

Industry observers note that sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, mentioned he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

“For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford noted.

Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

And he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

“We see that bipartisan process as extremely crucial to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” said Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, stated by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

Industry observers note that he stated GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

According to recent reports, the union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that as we get closer to final results from the 2026 midterms, the scale of the carnage comes more clearly into view. The question is not whether Republicans can recover from this, but whether the American system of government will be changed irreparably before they do. To what will Republicans return?

According to recent reports, in the Senate, Democrats gained nine seats, the biggest swing since Republicans’ nine-seat pickup in 2014. With 56 senators, it’s the Democrats’ biggest majority since 2009–10, when they peaked at 60 seats. Republicans haven’t had that many Senate seats since 1922, when the caucus was 59 seats after the 1920 landslide that repudiated Woodrow Wilson’s progressivism and swept Warren Harding into office. If you’re wondering, the largest-ever Republican Senate caucus, in absolute numbers rather than as a share of the chamber, was 60 in 1907; the largest Democratic caucus was 75 seats at the peak of the Fresh Deal in 1937. There’s a reason why Franklin D. Roosevelt thought he could get away with Court-packing with 75 senators.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

On “The Real Stakes of the Wilderness Years”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Africa Brief.

The highlights this week: Health leaders issue new warnings about the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, voters choose continuity in Cape Verde’s presidential election, and the board of an African literary prize exonerates a winner accused of using artificial intelligence.

Recent findings suggest that six months into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, the rare Bundibugyo variant of the virus reveals no sign of slowing down in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is exacerbated by an underfunded health system and armed conflict in eastern provinces, where global mining projects have led to increased disease transmission.

The outbreak is “still serious, and is still not under control,” said Jean Kaseya, the director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, or Africa CDC. The death toll since the outbreak began in May has passed 5,500 people, with more than 11,000 people infected, according to Congolese government figures released last week.

It has been revealed that infections are now spreading at double the rate as when the outbreak began, according to Kaseya. More than 80 percent of latest cases are emerging outside of known contact lists, and more than 65 percent of deaths have occurred outside of healthcare facilities, he added.

Kaseya called the lack of coordination between Congo’s government and foreign donors “a collective failure,” urging donors to release $1.6 billion in pledged aid.

It has been revealed that international donors have disbursed more than $962 million to organizations that are implementing Congo’s Ebola response. But around $700 million of that sum was unaccounted for as of last month, according to Kaseya. The Africa CDC said that it was too early to attribute this discrepancy to embezzlement, but an investigation is underway.

In 2020, Congo’s former health minister was convicted of embezzling more than $400,000 from funds intended to fight Ebola during the 2018-2020 outbreak.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Congolese health workers—who have not been paid for months—have gone on strike. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warned last week that ambulances had run out of fuel, staff were untrained, and that the Congolese government and United Nations agencies needed to “strengthen oversight and accountability.” MSF has called the outbreak “out of control.”.

For Congo, dealing with the Ebola crisis requires tackling systemic challenges beyond healthcare, including poverty, conflict, and inefficient governance. But Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi appears to be focused on cementing his grip on power. On Nov. 9, he signed a law that critics say could grant him a third term in office.

In a recent development, congo’s 2006 constitution allows a maximum of two presidential terms and explicitly prevents parliament from changing those rules under any circumstance. The upcoming law lowers the threshold for holding national referendums and permits constitutional overhauls through referendums “in case of absolute necessity.”.

Recent findings suggest that tshisekedi became president in January 2019; his second term ends in 2028. He has said that he is not seeking a third term but would serve one if given a mandate by voters. “I have not asked for a third term, but I tell you this: If the people want me to have a third term, I will accept,” Tshisekedi said in May.

On Nov. 1, the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, a new rebel alliance led by former Congolese President Joseph Kabila, sent a letter to U.S. officials and the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Congo warning that any constitutional changes could derail peace negotiations. Kabila’s alliance includes the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23.

In a recent development, the Trump administration negotiated a peace accord between Congo and Rwanda in December 2025 that seemed to prioritize securing U.S. access to Congo’s critical minerals over tackling domestic government reforms and bolstering a weak state. Expanded mining in Congo’s forests has increased human contact with animals that carry the Ebola virus, according to scientists.

Nearly one year on, amid an Ebola outbreak and on the precipice of further conflict, Congo is paying the price for the institutional neglect enshrined in the deal.

Recent findings suggest that wednesday, Nov. 18: An Egyptian court hears the retrial of Lina Attalah, the editor in chief of Mada Masr, on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The U.N. has described the charges against Attalah as an assault on press freedom.

It has been revealed that the U.N. Security Council hears a briefing from the International Criminal Court on its work in Libya.

Thursday, Nov. 19, to Saturday, Dec. 19: Dak’Art, the biennale of contemporary African art, returns to Dakar, Senegal.

Wednesday, Nov. 25: The U.N. Security Council is due to renew its sanctions targeting al-Shabaab and other armed groups in Somalia.

Recent findings suggest that amnesty report on South Sudan. A fresh report from Amnesty International accuses South Sudan’s government and U.N. peacekeepers of failing to act on advance warnings of a March massacre that killed more than 200 people. The report came ahead of an announcement that South Sudan would again delay general elections to February 2027.

It has been revealed that the elections were previously scheduled for Dec. 22. The South Sudanese government did not cite a reason for the move, but authorities have repeatedly pushed back elections since 2022 amid a power struggle between President Salva Kiir and his ousted former deputy, Riek Machar.

A 2018 power-sharing arrangement between Kiir and Machar  broke down last year after an attack on a military base in Upper Nile state by an armed group known as the White Army, which killed more than 250 soldiers. Kiir accused Machar and his party’s military wing of colluding with the White Army, which Machar denied.

Machar is at the moment on trial for charges including treason.

Industry observers note that cape Verde elections. Cape Verdean President José Maria Neves was reelected on Sunday, capturing more than 63 percent of the vote amid record low turnout, according to provisional results. Neves’s main challenger, former Justice Minister Joana Rosa—the country’s first woman presidential candidate—conceded on Monday.

The lack of opportunities for young people in Cape Verde was a major election topic. Rosa pledged to address issues facing young people, while Neves promised to organize a summit to address youth emigration. According to data released in July by Cape Verde’s statistics body, around 65 percent of people aged 15 to 35 remarked they intended to emigrate.

Neves’s party has dominated Cape Verdean politics since it gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

Recent findings suggest that madagascar’s ties to Russia. U.S. Africa Command’s deputy commander, John Brennan, warned against Madagascar’s strengthening ties with Russia last week, saying that Moscow is importing the “Sahel model” to the island.

“We are concerned about Russia wanting to proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent,” Brennan mentioned in a media briefing. Since the country’s 2025 coup, Russia has supplied the military-backed government with weapons—amid repeated calls from young Madagascans for a return to democracy.

Some Africans perceived Brennan’s comments as lecturing from the United States. “America is not talking to Russia as a partner. It is talking to Madagascar as a client,” Fortune Madondo wrote in Modern Ghana, suggesting that the United States might condition assistance to needy Madagascar on its allegiance.

The criticism underscored why it’s notable that U.S. officials consider how their comments land in Africa. If not framed carefully, they could play into Russia’s narrative that the United States is acting like a colonial power.

It has been revealed that ghana to boost local manufacturing. Ghana will invest $10 billion over four years in a domestically funded “new economy” program to boost local manufacturing and jobs. Ghanaian Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson told parliament in his 2027 budget speech last Friday that the funds will increase refining capacity and reduce lower-value raw materials exports.

Recent findings suggest that around $1.5 billion of the package will be allocated to financing refining facilities for gold, manganese, bauxite, and lithium. The Ghanaian government remarked it is relying on tax reforms already approved by parliament, better tax collection, and revenue from oil and minerals exports to finance the program.

The winner of this year’s 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza, has been cleared of using artificial intelligence to write his award-winning short story, “The Blue Fighter,” after an October article in the Atlantic noted that the AI detection software Pangram found the story was entirely AI-generated.

The Atlantic article sparked pushback from Africa’s literary community. Critics noted AI detection tools are disproportionately weaponized against authors from marginalized backgrounds. Following a monthlong review, the Caine Prize’s board said that digital forensic evidence revealed the article was human-written and that Kundizeza’s $13,000 award stands.

It has been revealed that nigeria’s surveillance state. An investigation by Ajibola Amzat for the Center for Collaborative Investigative Journalism found that Nigeria has spent billions of dollars of public funds on surveillance technology that is supposedly intended to fight insecurity—but is routinely used instead to monitor protesters, journalists, and government critics.

“Constitutionally guaranteed dissent is being watched and increasingly hunted while the terrorists and bandits freely operating in several corners of Nigeria’s 36 states remain elusive,” Amzat wrote.

According to recent reports, europe’s externalized borders. On Monday, five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands—announced looks to send asylum-seekers who have exhausted all legal avenues to Rwanda.

In 2024, the United Kingdom scrapped a similar deal due to legal challenges over the country’s human rights record. Since 2019, the European Union has also funded a scheme operated by the U.N. refugee agency that temporarily evacuates refugees from Libya to Rwanda.

In light of this week’s news, we’re revisiting Sally Hayden’s 2020 Foreign Policy dispatch from Rwanda’s refugee centers. “At what point does the EU become responsible for refugees it has forced from its borders through externalization policies?” Hayden wrote at the time.

#30819. Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1484 w)
