  • Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.
  • It has been revealed that the world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal.

It has been revealed that the world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

The story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

Recent findings suggest that the inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

Humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

According to recent reports, fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

The United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

In a recent development, that trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

In a recent development, this dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

There is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

Or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

Another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

In the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

Modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

Recent findings suggest that and modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

There are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

Apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal shows up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

Sources indicate that many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

Richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

It has been revealed that if the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.).

Sources indicate that the same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very rapidly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

According to recent reports, the coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: Fresh York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

According to recent reports, something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

Demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

But for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More important, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The new dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

Short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

In this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

If governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.

In a recent development, one of many ways to interpret the U.S. midterm results is that they were an opportunity for Americans to express their concerns about the war in Iran. In that reading of events, Tehran’s strategy to hurt U.S. President Donald Trump has had at least some impact. But now that the elections are over, what will change? Will Trump feel like he now has no electoral constraints, widening his range of options in the war? And will Tehran feel like it has lost some leverage?

Industry observers note that according to Vali Nasr, a longtime Iran watcher, Iranian leaders believe that sustained disruptions to the global economy serve as a lever to change the actions of Western leaders—and perhaps act as a future deterrent. “Iran sees the result of the U.S. elections as proof of this concept. Their strategy is to boil the frog gradually,” he mentioned on the latest episode of FP Live.

It has been revealed that one of many ways to interpret the U.S. midterm results is that they were an opportunity for Americans to express their concerns about the war in Iran. In that reading of events, Tehran’s strategy to hurt U.S. President Donald Trump has had at least some impact. But now that the elections are over, what will change? Will Trump feel like he now has no electoral constraints, widening his range of options in the war? And will Tehran feel like it has lost some leverage?

According to Vali Nasr, a longtime Iran watcher, Iranian leaders believe that sustained disruptions to the global economy serve as a lever to change the actions of Western leaders—and perhaps act as a future deterrent. “Iran sees the result of the U.S. elections as proof of this concept. Their strategy is to boil the frog gradually,” he mentioned on the latest episode of FP Live.

Nasr is a professor and former dean of the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University. He is the author of, most recently, Iran’s Grand Strategy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Industry observers note that ravi Agrawal: Let’s start with the U.S. point of view on the Iran war. The consensus has been that Trump has three options. He could escalate militarily, but that has very uncertain outcomes. He could spin a victory and get out, but the spin is . Or he could focus on diplomacy and try to return to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) we had last summer, but that is a lot of hard work. What do you think the White House strategy is now that the midterms are over?

Vali Nasr: I think the president is actually pursuing all three strategies at the same time. Leaning in on diplomacy does not mean that he’s setting aside war plans, and asking for war plans does not mean that he is doing less diplomacy. He doesn’t have any good choices.

In a recent development, ideally, Trump would end this war through a negotiated settlement, much like what happened in June, but he has to meet the Iranian price for doing that, which is actually quite steep for him. At the moment, the positions of the two are too far apart. The Iranians want him to first go back to the MOU and implement it before they talk about anything else, such as the nuclear concern. Trump, on the other hand, needs the nuclear issue to be at the forefront in order to justify why he went to war for nine months.

According to recent reports, war is also not really an option, because in order for war to be meaningful, Trump has to do something big. But something big opens the door to Iranian retaliation, particularly in the Persian Gulf, which could devastate the global economy in larger ways. I’m sure Trump is hearing from Chinese President Xi Jinping and Arab, Chinese, and Russian leaders that nobody wants that kind of damage to the global economy. So he’s settling for the third option, which is to let Iran sit under the blockade and do nothing. In my opinion, that’s not a strategy. That’s twiddling his thumbs.

Sources indicate that the blockade is not foolproof. Iran is getting oil out and making money. At the same time, the Strait of Hormuz is still under a lot of pressure. The Iranians have actually increased the number of attacks they’re making there. Furthermore, I don’t think it’s sustainable, financially or otherwise, for the U.S. Navy to maintain the blockade long term. It is quite financially and labor intensive for the Navy to do so, and it doesn’t have any bases in the Persian Gulf that could provide relief. If the Iranians are able to sustain themselves with the amount of holes that already exist, then, ultimately, this is not sustainable.

It has been revealed that in fact, if the blockade starts working in the way in which the U.S. treasury secretary and U.S. secretary of state say it will, then Iran is likely to escalate. So ultimately, this strategy that everybody thinks is settled on is not tenable in the long term. Either it will collapse under its own weight, or one or the other party is bound to disturb it, which might bring us back to war.

It has been revealed that RA: I imagine that you could have stated a lot of this two weeks ago. The significant change that has come in the last couple of weeks is, of course, the U.S. midterm election results. Come January, the Democrats will have power in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. They feel that part of the mandate from the American people is trying to find a way to end the war. What is your sense of how Congress might impact how Trump tries to prosecute the end of this war, or dilly-dally, as you said?

VN: One outcome of these elections is a much more visible push within the United States against the war. It’s not just that the American people have spoken. If there was any shadow of a doubt that they really, really disliked this war, it has been dashed, particularly within the Republican Party. They might now think that if the Republican Party is to have any chance in 2028, this war should end now.

Recent findings suggest that so there is a sense that there is more momentum for diplomacy after the election than there was before. In fact, when U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance wrote to Iran’s leadership, everybody noted, “That’s exactly what we thought the consequence would be of the drubbing the administration got.”.

But Trump is unpredictable. He has his own view of what’s in his interest as well as what’s in America’s interest. He may go back to a conflict with Iran, so we’re not out of the woods. But the Iranians know that the economic cost of the war is having a tangible political impact on America, as well as France and Germany, even if it is not being reflected in the stock market on a daily basis. Ultimately, these countries are likely to decide at some point that this war is not worth the political blowback it’s causing.

RA: I was going to come to how Tehran is gaming out the post-midterms scenario. You make the point that Iran may sense that it is getting some of what it wants—it is imposing costs. The flip side of that could be that the costs have been imposed, and Trump has now seen the worst of it. He seems to be doubling down. With nothing to lose, he may now be impervious to electoral pressure, meaning the Iranians may not have much leverage with him.

According to recent reports, VN: That’s very true. This is a gamble. It doesn’t mean that because the elections happened, the Iranians can declare victory and say, “OK, we humiliated President Trump, now let’s sit down and talk.” Yes, they had a big win in terms of the midterm results, but now they have to deal with Trump.

Industry observers note that I think the way they see it is that the decision to go to war is still uncomfortable for President Trump. It’s true that he’s not looking at another election, but the Republicans are looking at 2028. And ultimately, the longer this war goes on, the more the pressure it brings about, particularly if the next phase of the war is more destructive. The Iranians are broadcasting that loud and clear as a form of deterrence. They’re saying they’re going to wreak havoc on the region and the global economy, no holds barred.

Industry observers note that if that’s the case, then President Trump still has to think about his legacy. He has to think about the future of the Republican Party. And he has to consider that if he enters into a wider war with Iran and he still isn’t able to defeat it, the scale of his failure will be even greater than it is now.

In a recent development, until now, the most key factor on the American side hasn’t been some kind of a calculated, rational, technocratic national interest. It has been the psychology of one man from the get-go of deciding to go to war, to Trump’s various permutations.

Recent findings suggest that nobody—whether it’s the United States’ allies or Iran or China—can say with any certainty how Trump might actually act. So I think the Iranians are taking this one step at a time, reading the tea leaves and applying pressure where they can with Congress—particularly the new Congress coming in—to see whether they can avoid a big war and get a settlement that would benefit them.

The Iran war is most likely to end not with a bang, but with a whimper.

The U.S. military faces “profound” long-term readiness concerns, one expert said.

According to recent reports, RA: Let me put something to you that I’ve been hearing from Trump administration officials I’ve spoken to on background. They say that Iran’s hand has significantly weakened over the last few months. The reasons they point to are that the amount of Gulf crude going through Hormuz has actually dropped significantly, from 83 percent to 60 percent, because Gulf states are using pipelines more and relying less and less on Hormuz. The rial is down to 1.7 million to the dollar. Recent U.S. sanctions have targeted the regime explicitly, as opposed to targeting the Iranian people. They’ve shut down parts of Mahan Air, which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) relied on, as well as a United Arab Emirates branch of Banque Misr, which served the IRGC.

Sources indicate that there’s a sense in the White House—or at least, it’s their narrative—that these measures must really hurt the people in power in Iran, and at some point the pain will be so great that the regime will be forced to make different choices. Do you buy any of that?

VN: No, I don’t. This is largely self-serving, anecdotal rhetoric, which has gotten us to this point. I don’t see a sign that the degree of pressure that this administration thinks it is imposing on Iran is actually being felt there and changing attitudes. When Iran sent its diplomats to the United Nations, the proposal they presented to the United States was an expansion of the Islamabad-brokered MOU, changed in ways that benefited Iran more. The Iranians referred to it as “Islamabad-Plus.”.

Industry observers note that let’s also consider the fact that when Mecca defense alliance members and Pakistan’s army chief went to Tehran in October, Iran’s response to Vice President Vance’s letter was that Iran was sticking to its demands that Washington must fulfill all seven preconditions to resuming talks and reopening Hormuz. The United States’ pressure tactics are not working.

This administration doesn’t want to go to war or make a deal with Iran. They need to sell this “do nothing” strategy as a viable, working strategy, so they’re repackaging the blockade and saying it’s going to work this time. Two months ago, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was promising that there would be a run on the Iranian banks. That hasn’t happened. So I’m suspicious of these kinds of claims.

Sources indicate that iran is under a tremendous amount of pressure, but I don’t think the administration has a gauge of where the tipping point for them is. So it’s throwing a Hail Mary pass with more sanctions, hoping that they will do the trick, and then we get a lot of rhetoric trying to sell the current holding pattern as an actual strategy.

RA: So in response to everything you’re saying, Tehran’s strategy might be to wait out the next two years.

In a recent development, VN: If they have to, yes. Although, I don’t know. Iran’s supreme leader remarked in his last major statement that this “no war, no peace” situation is not sustainable or acceptable to Iran.

According to recent reports, when and how will Iran disturb this status quo? We don’t know. We can already see that they are escalating pressure on shipping. In the past week, more of the shuttle ships that the UAE has been using to ferry oil from inside tankers in the Persian Gulf to tankers in the Arabian Sea are being hit. The number of mines installed in the Strait of Hormuz has also increased. More oil might go out on some days than others. So the Iranians are making the situation more unstable.

Industry observers note that there is a difference between the way the West and Iran look at this situation. The U.S. and many observers think a move from Iran has to be really big to be meaningful. For instance, if they can’t bring the cost of oil to $200 a barrel, then they’ve lost.

But the Iranians actually do not look at things this way. Very early in the war, they understood that the price of oil is not 100 percent in their hands. What they believe works is sustained instability in the energy market. The costs of oil, natural gas, jet fuel, diesel, fertilizer, and so on are far above where they were. None of these measures by themselves will break the global economy, but if you put them together for long enough, they’re very effective.

Iran sees the result of the U.S. elections as proof of this concept. Their strategy is to boil the frog gradually. I think sometimes in the West we look at this and say, “Well, the frog is just sitting there and nothing’s happening to it, so the Iranians have failed.” So I think this is a race between whether Iran runs out of gas first or its strategy works.

Right now, I detect a certain degree of confidence from Iran. I don’t see the trepidation that observers on the outside are assuming the regime has. So either Iran has a good poker face, or it’s seeing the picture very differently than Washington does.

RA: It’s fascinating, and it’s always so hard to know whom or what to believe.

It has been revealed that I’m curious what you make of these reports that claim to be from U.S. intelligence suggesting that Iran is developing prepares to detonate a dirty bomb in Washington, D.C. These are just reports. Tehran, of course, denies that any of this is true, but I’m curious how you are reading that story and reacting to it.

VN: We’re in the midst of a war, and there’s a lot of disinformation. There are people in the United States or in Israel who want the United States to go back to war with Iran, to “finish the job,” so to speak. After the elections, which made it very obvious that the American public is firmly opposed to this war, you could only change that public opinion in favor of war if there was this kind of threat against America, or if you could posit that Iran is a deranged and crazy regime that must be taken out. So it could possibly be disinformation.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, Iranians have also been taking certain actions as a form of deterrence. I don’t know whether Iran actually released a cyberattack on refrigerators in France—French intelligence claims they did, though the Iranians deny it—but it’s a message. “If you attack us, then we have cyber capabilities that could paralyze your cities.”.

It’s a kind of deterrence tactic. It’s a similar case with Iran issuing warnings to air bases in the U.K., which ultimately got the United States to move its airplanes from two different air bases. Some of this benefits Iran, because it’s a way of saying, “Do not assume that the next war would be cost-free. Our reach is much farther than you assume.”.

It also suggests to me that Iran doesn’t want to go back to war. Rather, its game blueprint is to try to get the United States to come to the table to accept their terms.

#30805. Latest Update: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2475 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: China’s AI Diplomacy Is Working

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Newly introduced American Security.
  • Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI?
  • Industry observers note that beijing has long appreciated this dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DANIEL REMLER is a Senior Fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Newly introduced American Security. He served as AI Policy Coordinator in the Office of the Special Envoy for Critical and Emerging Technology at the State Department from 2023 to 2025.

And America Should Be Taking Notes.

Can the United States and China simultaneously cooperate and compete on AI? That is the question driving debates in Washington about the wisdom of pursuing talks on the subject with Beijing. The Biden administration paired sweeping technology restrictions with a narrow dialogue on risk, and the Trump administration has kept a channel open even as it has downplayed safety. Some experts go further. They hope that cooperation on safety can be siloed off from competition entirely, a belief as appealing as it is fanciful. Any dialogue on AI risk takes place within the broader strategic competition between the United States and China.

Industry observers note that beijing has long appreciated this dynamic. Much of Washington has not. Whereas the United States has shifted its approach to AI competition and safety across and within presidential administrations, Beijing has kept its AI diplomacy focused on gaining competitive advantage over the United States. China has taken part in international AI safety discussions, but it has used them, along with talks with the United States, to paint U.S. export controls as the main obstacle to cooperation. It has cast itself as the champion of the developing world, promising a Chinese-led AI ecosystem without technological or financial barriers as an alternative to a restrictive U.S.-led AI order. The pitch is working. A growing number of states are embracing China’s message, and Chinese open-weight models are gaining people across the developing world.

If the United States wants to maintain its lead and make meaningful progress on safety, it needs to treat the dialogue as part of the competition with China. To do so, it must ramp up pressure on China outside the talks and offer countries still choosing sides a more compelling vision for AI adoption and governance. And when U.S. and Chinese officials next meet, in November, Washington should test Beijing’s seriousness about safety. In short, the United States should approach AI diplomacy with the same strategic clarity China has.

Recent findings suggest that the Biden administration’s first round of advanced semiconductor export controls in October 2022 and the release of ChatGPT a month later signaled that the United States had taken an early lead in the AI competition and would act to weaken China’s AI industry. Washington and its allies also seized the diplomatic initiative, taking the first steps toward global AI governance. In May 2023, the G-7 began intense discussions on AI governance that would eventually produce a code of conduct for developers. Weeks later, the United Kingdom announced it would host the first global AI safety summit at Bletchley Park.

Sources indicate that china responded by rolling out a diplomatic script it has been honing ever since. Its core tenets first appeared in the Global AI Governance Initiative, published in October 2023. It called for countries to “put equal emphasis on development and security” (though it left security to be defined by individual states) and contrasted China’s focus on cooperation and development with U.S. export controls, attacking Washington for “creating barriers and disrupting the global AI supply chain through technological monopolies and unilateral coercive measures.” Despite Beijing’s growing body of AI regulations at home, the initiative offered little more than slogans on the technology’s risks.

According to recent reports, that basic formula—cooperation and development, set against U.S. restrictions, with little to say about risk—has guided China’s AI diplomacy for the last three years. In March 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a U.S.-led resolution on safe, secure, and trustworthy AI intended to appeal to both developed and developing countries. China supported the resolution, then introduced another resolution centered on help for poorer countries and “emphasizing that member states should enjoy equal opportunities” to develop and use AI. At a UN Security Council meeting on AI chaired by the United States in December that year, China’s UN ambassador, Fu Cong, once again counterposed Beijing’s stated interest in cooperation against “discriminatory barriers based on ideological differences.” In thinly veiled terms, Fu was charging that U.S. restrictions on China harmed the developing world.

To win the support of these countries as they built out their AI infrastructure, China needed a bloc of its own. In July 2025, Premier Li Qiang proposed the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which promised developing countries technology, training, and a greater say in writing global AI rules. In a speech marking its launch a year later, Chinese leader Xi Jinping called for “openness,” shorthand for access to U.S. chips and the adoption of Chinese open-weight models. After urging countries to take the risks of AI seriously, Xi added that they should, “in the meantime,” jointly oppose “overstretching the national security concept in the field of AI and placing one country’s security over that of others.” Cooperation on risks, in Xi’s telling, was subordinate to overcoming U.S. restrictions.

WAICO has rapidly gained standing among its target audience. An early endorsement by UN Secretary-General António Guterres lent it immediate credibility in the eyes of developing countries, and Chinese officials have since promoted WAICO in frequent speeches and in bilateral meetings with countries as varied as Brazil, Pakistan, and Serbia. Beijing has signaled that membership will come with perks. Its draft export controls on leading models, released in October, promise to help WAICO’s 37 members build their AI capabilities, suggesting members could have easier access to models restricted for the rest of the world.

Xi personally led this diplomatic offensive in the lead-up to the Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump in September. During a speech in Kyrgyzstan, he pledged to expand a Chinese AI center for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization that helps members build local language models and train engineers. In Cairo, he and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi signed agreements on AI, data centers, and semiconductors, which have become a staple of Xi’s trips abroad. And in Newly introduced Delhi, Xi proposed an open-source AI zone for BRICS members and told other leaders that a “small yard, high fences” approach would only “box oneself in and divide the world.” AI risks were nowhere on the agenda. The message instead was that U.S. restrictions would isolate Washington, not Beijing.

Sources indicate that much of the allure of China’s pitch rests on how the country’s developers share their technology. Chinese developers release their best models with open weights, which any government or organization can download, run on its own hardware, and adapt to its own language. For governments wary of depending on American companies whose exports Washington can restrict, open-weight models promise a greater degree of control. Chinese developers rarely conduct or publish the results of any safety testing for these models, leaving others to discover after release whether, for example, they can be used to launch cyberattacks or build weapons. But their accessibility allows Beijing to argue that any effort to contain the risks of Chinese models is an attempt to deny AI to the developing world.

China’s approach to bilateral AI talks with the United States has deflected discussions of risk just as assiduously as its global AI diplomacy has. In May 2024, the United States and China held talks in Geneva, which I joined as part of the U.S. delegation. The U.S. objective of the talks was to test whether an in-depth technical exchange with China on AI risk was possible. The answer was no. Chinese diplomats steered the discussion away from risks for hours and declined to even explain China’s own AI regulations beyond a superficial overview, despite having technical experts from the relevant agencies in the room.

Recent findings suggest that the Chinese position came through most clearly in the opening and closing remarks of the delegation’s most senior officials. They began with an appeal for cooperation on capacity-building projects in the developing world. They then cast U.S. technology restrictions as an attempt to contain China’s development and the U.S. emphasis on safety as a barrier preventing developing countries from accessing and using AI. The implication was clear—export controls were the primary impediment to cooperation on AI safety. The one concrete outcome, a November 2024 statement in which former President Joe Biden and Xi affirmed “the need to maintain human control over the decision to use nuclear weapons,” asked little of Beijing.

Industry observers note that this September, after the summit between Trump and Xi in Washington, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs published an “eight-point consensus,” Beijing’s account of what the two sides had agreed to. It described the dialogue as an exchange on the “risks and benefits” of AI. But whereas the White House framed the dialogue as a security matter, listing it alongside nuclear arms control, China’s Ministry of Commerce stressed instead that talks had taken place, and would continue, under the two countries’ economic and trade mechanism. Folded into trade talks, a dialogue on AI risks and benefits leaves Beijing free to parry U.S. requests on risks, such as limits on openly releasing models with dangerous capabilities, by demanding that Washington relax export controls.

Xi did propose to “jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” conveniently eliding China’s own frequent use of AI against the United States in various ways, such as hacking campaigns and influence operations. He added that AI should remain under human control and be developed for good, a principle Beijing has repeated since 2023 but about which it has offered little further detail or follow-through. More pointed was his insistence that future dialogue should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” and his request that Chinese companies be “treated fairly,” both implicit rebukes of U.S. restrictions.

This record suggests Beijing will come to future meetings, beginning with the next discussion in November, with proposals designed to put Washington in a bind. Although U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has made clear that export controls are not on the table, Beijing will raise them anyway. If Washington engages, Chinese negotiators will claim a standing channel where U.S. restrictions on AI technology are up for negotiation. If it refuses, Beijing will continue to evade U.S. entreaties on safety while accusing Washington of stifling opportunity for developing countries. It hopes that every round of the dialogue will further cement an impression among allies such as Japan and the Netherlands that Washington will trade away restrictions over their heads, and that they should accommodate China’s AI ambitions, too.

In a recent development, but Washington is in a stronger position than its diplomacy has let on. The world’s leading models are still American, and, together with allies, the United States controls key chokepoints in the semiconductor supply chain. Export controls on those chokepoints are not a bargaining chip and should be strengthened. Chinese AI companies regularly lament their lack of high-end chips and have resorted to smuggling chips and illicitly distilling U.S. models. U.S. developers also conduct increasingly extensive and transparent safety testing, which Chinese developers avoid. Taken together, these strengths give Washington the means to press Beijing and an attractive offer for the rest of the world. It should use them, advertising its rigorously tested models to compete for global adoption while pressuring China on safety in the dialogue.

According to recent reports, the first chance to apply that pressure is the next bilateral meeting. Washington should set two conditions for it and future meetings. Chinese developers must commit to publishing safety evaluations at least as extensive as those that leading U.S. developers publish today on equivalent benchmarks for the most serious risks, such as cyberattacks and biological weapons, and to disclosing previous and future incidents. The United States can make the same commitments, as its companies already publish such evaluations, increasingly disclose incidents, and open their models to independent and government evaluators before release. Otherwise, the incident channel to which the two sides agreed in September will run one way, with China free to point to U.S. incidents while reporting none of its own.

These conditions would change the terms of the dialogue. Since 2023, Washington has raised risks and Beijing has steered the conversation toward development. As long as Chinese companies face no scrutiny for the risks of their models, Beijing can tout them for their openness and innovation without having to answer questions from the rest of the world about their safety. Concordia AI, which tracks China’s AI ecosystem, found that only five of China’s ten leading developers published safety test results for any model over the past year, and none did so consistently. If China agrees, governments and companies choosing which models to use will be able to judge Chinese and American developers by the same criteria. If China refuses, the onus will be on Beijing to explain why fair treatment for Chinese companies should not extend to safety testing. Regardless, the U.S. government should ramp up its own tests of newly introduced Chinese models and publish the results. It should also avoid unforced errors, such as Trump’s waving away of AI safety concerns as a “hoax,” which hand Beijing an easy retort to U.S. appeals.

Sources indicate that more broadly, effective AI diplomacy ultimately requires convincing other countries to join the American AI ecosystem. Countries that train their engineers, build their local language models, and run their data centers on Chinese technology will come to depend on it. To counter that dependence (and prevent it from turning into political alignment), Washington needs to present a positive vision of AI governance that pairs verifiable safety commitments—the kind Chinese developers avoid—with the access and investment developing countries want.

U.S. companies already offer the best technology, but Washington has yet to put real diplomatic weight behind them. It should draw from its evolving approach at home to rally partners around shared safety measures. Under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, six leading U.S. companies committed themselves to internal controls, external audits, and independent oversight. The G-7 Code of Conduct, which built on voluntary commitments secured under the Biden administration, could incorporate the accord’s measures and serve as a common standard for partners. Countries that agree to its measures could receive priority for technology and financing. Without such incentives, the AI competition may be determined by price and access alone, where China has the edge.

It has been revealed that much of Washington has treated talks with Beijing as a place to manage the shared risks of AI apart from the competition. China has always treated them as an arena of the larger rivalry. To maintain its lead and make real progress on safety, the United States should start doing the same.

In Italy, Meloni Grapples With a Potential Spoiler

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

  • Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September. Her administration is now the longest-serving in Italy—and the most far-right—since World War II. Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, rules in a coalition with the populist League and center-right Forza Italia.

In a recent development, A pamphlet handed out at the Bari rally highlighted Meloni’s economic and immigration policies, a major public housing proposal, proposals to build fresh prisons, and a push to reintroduce nuclear power. Missing among the milestones was any mention of Italy’s support for Ukraine.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni celebrated the fourth anniversary of her government with a large rally in the port city of Bari in September. Her administration is now the longest-serving in Italy—and the most far-right—since World War II. Meloni, who leads the far-right Brothers of Italy party, rules in a coalition with the populist League and center-right Forza Italia.

A pamphlet handed out at the Bari rally highlighted Meloni’s economic and immigration policies, a major public housing proposal, proposals to build new prisons, and a push to reintroduce nuclear power. Missing among the milestones was any mention of Italy’s support for Ukraine.

That absence is no coincidence. Meloni is now grappling with a challenger further to her right on many challenges: Roberto Vannacci, a former general who leads the ultranationalist, pro-Russian National Future party. His influence is putting the prime minister in a difficult position with voters and shaping her political choices, especially on Ukraine—already seen as a weak point for Meloni.

Sources indicate that vannacci rose to national prominence in 2023 with a bestselling self-published book, The World Upside Down, that railed against LGBTQ rights, feminism, immigration, and environmentalism. He was elected to the European Parliament the next year with the League, but in January, he left the party to found his own.

Recent findings suggest that amid pressure from Vannacci and his party, Meloni’s government has hardened its line on immigration; passed law-and-order measures targeting violent protests, vandalism, and illegal gatherings; and expanded legal protections for police. The prime minister also backed a controversial antisemitism bill, approved by Parliament this week, that opponents say conflates criticism of Israel with anti-Jewish sentiment.

It has been revealed that until recently, Meloni had no serious rivals, and her Brothers of Italy party led every poll. Though Vannacci’s National Future is now losing some ground, he could still serve as a spoiler for Meloni. Her party’s rightward shift could even hand the divided center-left an unexpected victory in the general elections that are due next year.

Brothers of Italy, which Meloni co-founded in 2012, has roots in the former Italian Social Movement (MSI)—a neofascist party that emerged from the remnants of Benito Mussolini’s regime in 1946. Meloni has never disavowed those origins, arguing that MSI was a “party of the democratic right” even as she has distanced herself from historical fascism.

Sources indicate that meloni’s coalition partners have helped her project that image of distance, to varying degrees. Forza Italia, which is a member of the center-right European People’s Party, defines itself as the moderate wing of the coalition. The League doesn’t have fascist roots but tries to outflank Brothers of Italy on the right on certain issues.

Industry observers note that for the past 30 years, no far-right party has succeeded as a permanent force in Italy outside of the center-right coalition. Elsewhere in Europe, the far right has solidified its presence and destabilized mainstream politics—including the National Rally in France, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, and Britain’s Reform UK.

It has been revealed that italy no longer seems to be immune to that trend. “We were convinced that the right stopped at Giorgia Meloni. Evidently, that was not the case,” said Mattia Diletti, a political scientist at Sapienza University of Rome. He compared National Future to the AfD due to the “strong value placed on national identity and national culture, as well as its strongly anti-European spirit.”.

Much of Vannacci’s platform echoes nationalist-populist positions espoused by Meloni and her allies before she came to power. He explicitly endorses “remigration”—the large-scale deportation of migrants and asylum-seekers as well as long-term residents and those born in Europe but deemed “unassimilated.” Vannacci has described Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as an “existential war” for Russians, arguing that NATO’s eastward expansion forced it into a war.

In a recent development, just 10 years ago, Meloni openly cited the “great replacement” conspiracy theory. She called for an end to sanctions against Moscow as recently as February 2022, days before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. On the campaign trail that year, Meloni exploited anti-establishment sentiment and presented herself as an underdog, allowing her to build a base as the left wing fractured.

However, the prime minister has governed as a more moderate leader than expected. Since taking office, Meloni has insisted to other European Union countries that she is no longer pro-Russia or Euroskeptic, embracing a pro-Ukraine stance and making several trips to Kyiv. She has maintained a cautious economic approach, focusing more on balancing the budget and adhering to European Commission procedures than on public investment.

While Brussels appreciated this pivot, it was not welcomed by her whole base.

According to recent reports, “Meloni has become institutionalized, and many of her voters have not liked this,” mentioned Martina Carone, a pollster at Italy’s YouTrend. “People are struggling with rising petrol prices and the cost of living … it’s difficult to convince voters that things are getting better by presenting them with statistics.”.

Italy’s center-left, for its part, has struggled to overcome divisions between the Democratic Party and the populist Five-Star Movement over foreign policy, the environment, and the economy. Facing a fragmented opposition, Meloni long maintained enough support to avoid a serious challenge.

But she suffered a significant defeat in March, when voters rejected a constitutional reform proposed by her government. The emergence of Vannacci’s party, precisely as Meloni sought to project strength, is “exactly the kind of unexpected development that throws her intends into disarray,” mentioned Massimo Rebotti, a political journalist. Vannacci is borrowing from Meloni’s own opposition tactics: criticizing those in power without bearing any responsibility for governing.

In a recent development, national Future surged in the polls in August and September before slumping more recently. But even on the margins, it could pose a threat to Meloni in next year’s general elections. Around two-thirds of Italy’s parliamentary seats are distributed proportionally in multimember districts; the remaining seats are filled in single-member districts using a first-past-the-post system. Meloni’s coalition is particularly vulnerable in these single-member constituencies.

According to recent reports, if the center-left wins enough of those districts, then Meloni’s current coalition could fail to win a parliamentary majority. Meloni could instead form an electoral alliance with National Future. But that would put her in a sticky position with European allies, who are wary of a party described by the Financial Times as “Russia’s ‘Trojan horse’ in Italy.”.

Though there is no documented link between Vannacci and the Kremlin, the National Future leader has praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for restoring the country’s wealth and international standing. His foreign-policy platform aligns with that of Moscow: He opposes EU rearmament, wants to restore economic ties with Russia, and has called on Ukraine to accept Russian peace terms.

Meloni has publicly ruled out allying with anyone who opposes support for Ukraine. After all, an alliance with Vannacci would erode the credibility that Meloni has built in Brussels as a fixture at meetings of the so-called “coalition of the willing,” with potentially significant financial consequences.

In a recent development, in June, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen signaled her openness to Meloni’s request for more budget flexibility, allocating 14 billion euros over three years to mitigate increasing energy costs. The arrangement relies on the EU’s national escape clause, which allows states to deviate from approved expenditure plans by up to 0.3 percent of GDP annually due to exceptional circumstances.

Created to accommodate increased defense spending amid the war in Ukraine, the clause has been extended to account for energy security as well. The EU also quietly let Italy off the hook when it overshot its debt-to-GDP ratio last year above the bloc’s fiscal ceiling. If Meloni were to let Vannacci—who opposes the EU rearmament strategy—into her coalition, these concessions would likely be impossible for Brussels to justify.

Recent findings suggest that in October, facing a threat from Vannacci’s party, Meloni’s coalition pushed through an electoral law that scraps most of the single-member constituencies ahead of next year’s elections. The new law includes a bonus system to hand whichever coalition or electoral list that exceeds 42 percent of the vote 70 extra seats in the lower house and 35 extra seats in the Senate to reach a governing majority. If no coalition reaches that threshold, then seats are allocated proportionally.

Meloni is also still shifting her policies to the right to connect with extreme factions within her base. In July, the prime minister proposed a law to make minors between the ages of 14 and 18 automatically presumed to be criminally liable. She has proposed a cap on foreign students in classrooms and a burqa ban.

In a recent development, the prime minister is also cautiously recalibrating her stance on Ukraine. At the beginning of her term, Meloni made political and military support for Kyiv an unequivocal objective of her foreign policy. At the time, more than half of Italians were willing to back Ukraine. As that support began to wane, Meloni could still afford to prioritize her standing with allies abroad over potential discontent at home, given that there was no opposition capable of unseating her.

According to recent reports, now, however, Meloni talks about Ukraine as little as possible. Only 28 percent of Italians support arming Ukraine today, according to an Ipsos poll; it is particularly unpopular among right-wing voters. According to Rebotti, aid to Ukraine is Vannacci’s matter to exploit, since his party “can call for the money being spent to be used in other ways, from healthcare to security to education.”.

In recent months, Meloni has stated that she is opposed to providing Ukraine with more effective offensive weapons and expressed reservations about Kyiv joining the EU. She postponed the delivery of an aid package in August, disrupting an established six-month schedule. Meloni said the package would only contain power generators, but Italian media reports that it included weapons.

It has been revealed that italy’s bilateral aid to Ukraine has always been modest, amounting to just 0.24 percent of its GDP, which places it 18th of 27 EU countries. The risk is more symbolic: A founding member of both the Group of Seven and the EU cutting back its assistance to Kyiv would weaken the narrative of unity that the EU has built up as U.S. President Donald Trump has scaled back aid to Ukraine. It would also give a boost to pro-Russian parties across Europe that hope for similar pullbacks.

To win in 2027, Meloni must solve a nearly impossible equation. Allying with Vannacci could guarantee a majority but cost her major international support. Refusing that alliance could split the right-wing vote, either costing her power or producing a hung parliament and leaving Meloni dependent on the center-left. The question is whether Meloni’s rightward shift will be enough to navigate that narrow path.

Giorgio Ghiglione is a freelance writer in Milan. His work has appeared in the Guardian, Al Jazeera, and Internazionale. X: @giorgioghiglion.

Shenzhen Was No Yalta Conference

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.

Still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.

The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.

China and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.).

Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a fresh Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.

It has been revealed that this speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a upcoming Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.

In a recent development, crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.

The Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.

Nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.

According to recent reports, for all the talk of a upcoming world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.

The joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.

But Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, problems involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.

It has been revealed that takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi stated a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.

Industry observers note that as other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.

Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.

A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A New Manual, one of the most important books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.

Recent findings suggest that wilkinson is now 85, but each new edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.

A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.

Nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the tech giant facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.

In a recent development, reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.

Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.

U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.

According to recent reports, but it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.

#30799. Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3536 w)
📖 Baca
